growth_story.headline: Germany's export-led revival after the post-unification stall has faded: income per person is about where it first was in 2017.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, income per person in Germany has grown 1.2 percent a year on average, and the data find no lasting shift in that pace, so the whole period reads as one era. Within it, unification gave a short lift, with growth of 4.4 percent in 1990 and 4.3 percent in 1991, before income per person fell 1.6 percent in 1993 and stalled again in 2002 and 2003. From the mid-2000s a strong world economy and reforms that restored competitiveness drove an export revival: growth reached 4.0 percent in 2006, income per person fell 5.3 percent in 2009 when world trade collapsed, then bounced back by 4.3 percent in 2010 and 5.7 percent in 2011. The last decade has been slower, with growth of 0.5 percent a year over 2016-2025 against 1.6 over 2006-2015. After a fall of 4.2 percent in 2020 and a rebound, income per person peaked in 2022, then fell in 2023 and 2024 after an energy-price shock and a fast rise in interest rates to bring inflation down; in 2025 it was 1.5 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 2017.

threads.title: Unification boost, then a swoon
threads.text: Unification lifted income per person by 4.4 percent in 1990 and 4.3 percent in 1991, but the boom did not last. Income per person fell 1.6 percent in 1993, and growth stalled again in 2002 and 2003.

citations.title: Tests of German Resilience (IMF Working Paper WP/12/239)
citations.quote: The unification of West and East Germany in 1990 provided a short domestic boost, but then the German economy again went into a swoon.

threads.title: Export revival and the 2009 collapse
threads.text: From the mid-2000s, a strong world economy and reforms that restored competitiveness helped German exporters win back ground, and growth reached 4.0 percent in 2006. The world trade collapse cut income per person by 5.3 percent in 2009, before a quick rebound in 2010 and 2011.

citations.title: Tests of German Resilience (IMF Working Paper WP/12/239)

citations.title: Tests of German Resilience (IMF Working Paper WP/12/239)

threads.title: Energy shock and dearer money
threads.text: Income per person peaked in 2022, then fell 1.0 percent in 2023 and 0.8 percent in 2024. The IMF links this to the jump in energy prices in mid-2022 and the fast rise in interest rates that followed to bring inflation down.

threads.title: Tougher export markets, slow productivity
threads.text: Growth of income per person slowed from 1.6 percent a year over 2006-2015 to 0.5 over 2016-2025. The sources point to weak productivity growth, stiffer competition in export markets, including from China, and new trade barriers.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 0.3 percent in 2025, after falling in 2023 and 2024. The IMF dates the start of a recovery to late 2024 and expects the 2025 reform of the debt-brake rule, the legal limit on government borrowing, to help drive it, while new trade-related headwinds have slowed the pace.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation with Germany

growth_story.tension: The data read 1990-2025 as a single era at 1.2 percent a year, because no shift in the pace reaches 2 points. The sources tell distinct chapters instead: a swoon after unification, an export-led revival from the mid-2000s, and recent stagnation. The slowdown they describe does show in the decade averages, 1.6 then 0.5 percent a year, but it is too small for the tool to mark a new era.
